summary: Notes that implementations handle well-known BGP communities inconsistently, which makes life hard for operators. It recommends that implementors not add further inconsistency going forward, and it updates RFC 1997. It asks operators to deploy consistent community handling while accounting for the differences that exist today.

plainLanguage.summary: Different routers follow special tags on messages in different ways, which confuses the people running them. This tells makers to stop making it worse and to treat the tags alike.

subtitle: Routers disagree about what a 'set community' command does to well-known BGP communities; this RFC documents the mess and freezes it.

tldr.problem: RFC 1997 did not say how well-known communities may be changed by operator policy, so vendors made different choices, and the same 'set community' configuration behaves differently on different routers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC records how several popular implementations treat the 'set' directive, then requires vendors to document their behavior and never change how a given community is treated when it later becomes well-known.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 1997 and is a Proposed Standard. It does not fix the existing differences. Operators are told to limit use of 'set' and to confirm with a neighbor how a community will be treated.

facts.label: IOS XR communities kept by set

today: RFC 8642 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1997, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It documents behavior as of its 2019 publication and does not itself change the vendor differences it describes.

sections.title: Why Well-Known Communities Needed a Policy Note
sections.content:
RFC 1997 introduced the BGP Communities attribute and the idea of well-known communities. In hindsight, the RFC says, it did not prescribe as fully as it should have how operator policies may manipulate those communities.

Implementations therefore differ, and the differences produce inconsistent behavior that operators find hard to identify and resolve. This document describes the differences to help operators write consistent policies in a multi-vendor network and to stop new divergence. Its key requirement is that BGP implementors MUST NOT create further inconsistencies from this point forward.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a rule book that forgot to say what to do with some special stickers. Every company guessed differently, and now people get mixed up. This note says: stop guessing differently.

sections.title: Replacing Communities with 'set'
sections.content:
RFC 1997 says a BGP speaker receiving a route with the COMMUNITIES path attribute may modify it according to local policy. Adding or removing communities is one basic need. This RFC focuses on another: replacing all communities with a new set.

Most BGP policy implementations offer a set syntax that operators use to mean 'remove any and all communities on the route and apply this set instead'. Some operators instead write 'delete community *:*' followed by 'add community x:y' statements. The same differences exist in both forms, so the RFC refers only to each implementation's 'set' directive.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want to peel off every sticker on a package and put on new ones. Routers have a command for that, and it is this command that behaves differently from brand to brand.

sections.title: How Vendors Differ
sections.content:
Vendor implementations differ in how they treat certain well-known communities when the 'set' syntax is used. Some replace all communities, including the well-known ones, with the new set. Others replace all non-well-known communities but leave any well-known ones on the route. The result is that identical-looking policy can produce very different outcomes on different platforms.

The RFC documents observed behavior in several implementations:

  • Juniper Junos OS: 'community set' removes all communities, well-known or otherwise.
  • Cisco IOS XR: 'set community' removes all communities except a short list (see the table below). Well-known communities can be removed only by naming them one at a time, for example 'delete community accept-own'.
  • Extreme Brocade NetIron: 'set community X' removes all communities and sets X.
  • Huawei VRP: 'community set' removes all communities, well-known or otherwise.
  • OpenBGPD: 'set community' does not remove any communities, well-known or otherwise.
  • Nokia SR OS: its 'replace' keyword replaces all communities, well-known or otherwise, with the specified ones.

Operators are advised to consult vendor documentation for full details.
sections.plainLanguage: One brand's eraser wipes every sticker, another brand's skips a few special ones, and one brand's eraser wipes nothing at all. Same button, different results.

sections.title: The Cisco IOS XR Exception List
sections.content:
Cisco IOS XR keeps six communities when 'set community' runs: 0:0 (internet), 65535:0 (graceful-shutdown), 65535:1 (accept-own), 65535:65281 (NO_EXPORT), 65535:65282 (NO_ADVERTISE) and 65535:65283 (NO_EXPORT_SUBCONFED, also called local-AS).

The RFC also notes an inconsistency. This list diverges from the IANA registry of well-known communities: many communities on the IANA list get no special treatment in IOS XR, and 0:0 is not formally a well-known community at all, because it is not in the IANA registry and comes from the Reserved range. The RFC says this merely notes an inconsistency and is not a plea to protect the whole IANA list from 'set community'.
sections.plainLanguage: One brand keeps six special stickers no matter what. But its list does not match the official list of special stickers, and the RFC just points that out.

sections.title: What Vendors, Operators and RFC Authors Must Do
sections.content:
The RFC says it would be operationally disruptive for vendors to change their current implementations, so it does not ask for that. Instead:

  • Vendors MUST clearly document the behavior of the 'set' directive.
  • Vendors MUST ensure that the 'set' treatment of any specific community does not change if that community becomes a new well-known community through future standardization. For most implementations 'set' must keep removing it; where 'set' removes nothing, that must continue.
  • Operators are encouraged to limit use of 'set' (within reason) to improve consistency across platforms.
  • Operators are urged never to rely on an implicit understanding of a neighbor ASN's community handling. Before announcing prefixes with NO_EXPORT or any other community, confirm with the neighbor how it will be treated.
  • Authors of RFCs defining similar attributes (large communities, wide communities and so on) should state explicitly how the new attribute is to be handled.
sections.plainLanguage: Makers must write down what their eraser does and never change it for a sticker later. People using the routers should ask their neighbors what will happen to their stickers before relying on them.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: surprising defaults and undocumented behaviors are not good for security, and this document attempts to remedy that by getting behavior documented.

For IANA, the document was listed as an additional reference for the registry of BGP well-known communities. No new values are defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Surprises are bad for safety. Writing down what each router does means fewer surprises.
